claims.text: The target material is a solid-solution HEA containing at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 at.% each.
The target material is a homogeneous, single-phase bcc alloy outside Nb-Ta-dominated and overly titanium-rich material classes.
Replacing part of one constituent with a larger-radius element of similar chemical character will increase atomic size mismatch.
Increased atomic size mismatch will enhance local lattice distortion in the bcc lattice.
The substitution-induced lattice distortions will remain uniformly distributed if the alloy remains single phase.
Increased lattice distortion will modify the electronic density of states near the Fermi level.
Increased lattice distortion will strengthen electron-phonon coupling.
Stronger electron-phonon coupling will raise the superconducting transition temperature.
Excessive disorder may induce electronic localization or phase separation.
Phase separation or ordering may negate the proposed increase in superconducting transition temperature.
Arc melting under an inert atmosphere ensures homogeneous mixing and formation of a single bcc phase.
Electrical resistivity and magnetic measurements can be used to characterize the superconducting transition and bulk superconductivity.
The modified alloy will have a higher superconducting transition temperature than the unmodified baseline alloy.
The increase in superconducting transition temperature may be approximately 1-2 K.
The proposed effect applies only within the composition window that retains a homogeneous, single-phase bcc structure at ambient pressure.
The magnitude of the transition-temperature change depends on substitution level and the balance between electron-phonon coupling and disorder-induced scattering.
A controlled comparison can replace approximately 10 at.% of one constituent while retaining every element above 5 at.%.
Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in transition temperature in a phase-pure modified alloy would falsify the hypothesis.
Detecting phase separation or ordering after substitution would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary field excludes phase-separated or ordered samples from the hypothesis's domain, whereas the falsification rule treats phase separation or ordering as falsification. Such a result would instead show that the intervention violated the stated boundary condition and would not decisively test the proposed mechanism within a single-phase bcc alloy.
